narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 69% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the admissions decision treated you as more likely than not to struggle at the licensing stage, which outweighed your other qualifications.

The strongest factor was your third-year academic decile: you are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the middle of the sixth decile. That very low third-year standing pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score of 20 was the second most influential factor; it is far below the accepted-student average of about 37 and also pushed toward a failure prediction. Your lower-middle family-income background was the third most important factor, but it leaned toward passing rather than failing. It was not enough to offset the academic and test-score signals.

To improve your chances, focus first on the areas the decision most depended on. Retake the LSAT only after substantial preparation and aim for a score much closer to the accepted range. Speak with admissions or pre-law advising about whether additional coursework, a later application, or an explanatory addendum about your record would be appropriate. Ask whether reconsideration or a conditional pathway is possible, and plan to reapply after you have concrete evidence of stronger academic and test performance.
